hunt.justification: EBPF rootkits undermine the integrity of local security tools by lying at the kernel level. Only a cross-surface comparison between the network fabric and the endpoint can reliably detect these 'ghost' signals. A negative result confirms that the introspection tools used by the SOC remain trustworthy.

meta.analysis: A standard detection rule can alert on the use of 'bpftool' or 'strace', but only a hunt can perform the stateful comparison between fabric-level network flows and host-level sockets to find discrepancies that a local agent cannot see on its own.

stages.name: Malicious file execution
observables: Execution of dropper or eBPF loader binary
Loading of eBPF programs into the kernel

stages.name: Hiding active network connections
observables: Manipulation of Netlink socket responses using bpf_probe_write_user
Inflation of nlmsghdr length fields in ss -tn output
Discrepancy between ss utility output and actual established TCP connections

stages.name: Hiding eBPF program IDs
observables: Injection of -ENOENT return value via bpf_override_return
Plaintext logs in /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe containing 'BPF cmd: %d, start_id: %u'
Truncated output in bpftool prog list enumeration

stages.name: Anti-debugging and ptrace blocking
observables: sys_enter_ptrace tracepoint intercepting PTRACE_ATTACH (0x10) or PTRACE_SEIZE (0x4206)
Automated delivery of SIGKILL (9) to processes attempting to trace specific PIDs

scenario.summary: eBPF rootkits such as VoidLink and LinkPro evade detection by manipulating kernel-to-userspace memory and return values to hide network connections and malicious eBPF programs. These tools utilize specific eBPF helpers like bpf_probe_write_user and bpf_override_return to spoof system utility outputs and protect malicious processes from being traced.

meta.rationale: Focus on high-value Linux targets: database servers, domain controllers (if Linux-based), and bastion hosts. These are the most likely targets for persistent rootkits.
meta.hypothesis: An adversary has deployed an eBPF rootkit that hides C2 connections from local network utilities like 'ss' and prevents forensics by killing debugging tools like 'strace' or 'bpftool'.

known_debuggers.description: Common introspection and debugging tools targeted by rootkits.

blind_spots.risk: Without fabric-level logs, we only see what the (potentially compromised) OS reports. A rootkit hiding from Netlink will hide from our agent as well.
blind_spots.question: whether outbound traffic exists that the OS is hiding
blind_spots.requires: VPC Flow Logs or network-layer telemetry in hb_network_connection (state_kind = 'log')

blind_spots.risk: If the malware author removes debug logging (bpf_printk), the 'tracing-pipe-access' indicator disappears.
blind_spots.question: whether the malware is logging its evasion attempts to trace_pipe
blind_spots.requires: bpf_printk being enabled/used by the malware

hunt.name: eBPF Rootkit Introspection Bypass
hunt.description: Linux rootkits like VoidLink and LinkPro use eBPF helpers like `bpf_probe_write_user` and `bpf_override_return` to manipulate kernel responses before they reach userspace. This hunt identifies these rootkits by finding 'ghost' connections—outbound traffic visible to the network fabric but absent from endpoint socket snapshots—and by stack-counting anomalous terminations of system introspection tools that suggest automated evasion.

config.content: SELECT hostname, device_uid, os_name, os_version FROM hb_devices WHERE LOWER(platform) = 'linux' AND lifecycle_state = 'running'
config.description: Identify all Linux hosts in the estate to narrow the subsequent behavioural queries.
config.expected_signal: A list of Linux hostnames. Silence means no Linux hosts are enrolled, making this hunt inapplicable.

primitive_config.label: Scope Linux estate
primitive_config.content: SELECT hostname, device_uid, os_name, os_version FROM hb_devices WHERE LOWER(platform) = 'linux' AND lifecycle_state = 'running'
primitive_config.expected: A list of Linux hostnames. Silence means no Linux hosts are enrolled, making this hunt inapplicable.

config.content: SELECT device_hostname, dst_endpoint_ip, dst_endpoint_port, protocol, COUNT(CASE WHEN state_kind = 'log' THEN 1 END) AS fabric_flow_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN state_kind = 'live' THEN 1 END) AS agent_socket_count FROM hb_network_connection WHERE time >= datetime('now', '-{{lookback_days}} days') AND direction = 'outbound' GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 HAVING fabric_flow_count > 5 AND agent_socket_count = 0 ORDER BY fabric_flow_count DESC
config.description: Find network traffic (flows) that exist at the fabric layer but are never reported as open sockets by the endpoint agent, suggesting local hiding.
config.expected_signal: Rows where the network sees traffic but the OS claims no socket exists. This is the primary indicator of a Netlink-level rootkit like VoidLink.

config.content: SELECT device_hostname, process_name, process_cmd_line, user_name, COUNT(*) as kill_events FROM hb_process_activity WHERE activity_id = 2 AND (instr(',' || '{{known_debuggers}}' || ',', ',' || LOWER(process_name) || ',') > 0 OR instr(',' || '{{known_debuggers}}' || ',', ',' || LOWER(process_path) || ',') > 0) AND time >= datetime('now', '-{{lookback_days}} days') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 HAVING kill_events > 1
config.description: Count terminations of debugging and network tools; rootkits often deliver SIGKILL to these processes to prevent discovery.
config.expected_signal: A high count of 'ss' or 'strace' terminations on a single host. In the context of eBPF rootkits, this indicates a defensive hook firing.

config.content: SELECT device_hostname, process_name, process_cmd_line, file_path, time FROM hb_file_activity WHERE (LOWER(file_path) = '/sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe' OR LOWER(file_path) LIKE '%/trace_pipe') AND time >= datetime('now', '-{{lookback_days}} days')
config.description: Detect processes reading from the trace_pipe, where LinkPro-style rootkits inadvertently stream their debug logs.
config.expected_signal: Any process reading the tracing pipe. While often legitimate for admins, it is used by rootkit userspace components to receive status updates.

config.objective: Determine if a host is showing signs of eBPF rootkit activity by weighing 'ghost' connections against anti-debugging signals.
config.description: Correlate ghost connections with debugger kills to confirm rootkit presence.
config.expected_signal: A per-host verdict linking disparate indicators of evasion.
config.success_criteria: A verdict of malicious | suspicious | benign per host with evidence citations.

config.question: the triage verdict is malicious or suspicious for at least one host
config.condition: the triage verdict is malicious or suspicious for at least one host
config.description: Direct the hunt based on the agent's confidence.
Contain the threat once high-confidence evidence of rootkit presence is found.
config.instructions: Isolate the host from the network immediately. Capture a full memory dump before rebooting, as eBPF programs live in kernel memory.

config.description: Final manual check of the evidence, especially the discrepancy between fabric and agent telemetry.
config.instructions: Compare the destination IPs found in the fabric logs against your threat intelligence. If the IPs are known C2 and are missing from the endpoint's socket logs, this is a confirmed rootkit. Verify if 'bpftool' is present on the host and whether it fails to run.
Note the hosts examined and the lack of ghost connections. Schedule a periodic re-run of the fabric vs. agent comparison.
